title: English Vocabulary 3 · Units 99–100
description: B2 signs, official notices and condensed newspaper English, including formal-register contrast, headline grammar, dramatic news vocabulary and wordplay.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study from the supplied textbook. Teaching targets and language contrasts were checked against the source; example sentences, Portuguese translations and usage notes are original, and textbook exercises and extended passages are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Textbook teaching pages 204–207 (PDF pages 205–208), including pictured signs and notices, the headline word table, exercises 99.1–99.4 and 100.1–100.4, and corresponding answer-key entries on PDF pages 256–257.
audit.pronunciation: Conservative broad British IPA for high-confidence simple words. Unreliable phrase transcriptions and abbreviations are left without IPA.
audit.languagePolicy: English throughout except Brazilian Portuguese translations under pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Checked text and rendered source-page visuals, compared exercise answers, reviewed word meanings and usage distinctions, and validated required structure, IDs and speech-target suitability.
audit.limitations: No actual browser import, TTS playback, recognition or bundled audio test. Source-aligned sign/register and headlines are not necessarily natural for everyday spoken English.

units.title: Unit 99 — The language of signs and notices
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 99. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Notices, signs, public information, restrictions and formal directives
learningObjectives: Interpret short public notices in natural everyday English.
Distinguish formal sign vocabulary such as alight, dismount, prohibited, prosecute and refrain from.
Understand admissions, trespassing, fines, shopping notices, parking restrictions and vacancies.
Recognise verb patterns and context-dependent meanings in public signage.

sectionsChecked: Teaching page including illustrated signs or tables

items.pt: descer de um veículo de transporte público
items.section: Signs and notices · Public transport and roads
items.example: Passengers should alight at the next stop for the museum.
items.note: A formal verb for getting off a bus or train; less common in everyday conversation than get off.

items.pt: descer de (ônibus, trem ou outro meio de transporte)
items.section: Signs and notices · Public transport and roads
items.example: Please alight from the train on the left-hand side.
items.note: Use alight from with the vehicle; alight at with a stop or station.

items.pt: descer de um veículo ou bicicleta
items.section: Signs and notices · Public transport and roads
items.example: We need to get off at the next station.
items.note: More common and conversational than alight when talking about buses and trains.

items.section: Signs and notices · Public transport and roads
items.example: No private vehicles may enter the courtyard.
items.note: Formal/general word for a means of transport; not limited to cars.

items.section: Signs and notices · Public transport and roads
items.example: Drivers must reduce speed near the school.
items.note: A directive found on road signs, often shortened to an imperative.

items.pt: rua sem saída para tráfego de passagem
items.section: Signs and notices · Public transport and roads
items.example: This is a no through road, so drivers cannot continue to the next street.
items.note: British road-sign language; a dead end does not provide a route through for vehicles.

items.section: Signs and notices · Public transport and roads
items.example: Motor vehicles cannot use this narrow path.
items.note: A vehicle powered by an engine or motor, as opposed to a bicycle in many traffic contexts.

items.pt: pague e deixe o comprovante visível
items.section: Signs and notices · Public transport and roads
items.example: The car park uses a pay and display ticket system.
items.note: British parking instruction: pay for a ticket and display it as required.

items.pt: desmontar; descer da bicicleta ou do cavalo
items.section: Signs and notices · Public transport and roads
items.example: Please dismount before entering the pedestrian zone.
items.note: Formal command for getting off a bicycle, motorbike or horse.

items.section: Signs and notices · Public transport and roads
items.example: Cyclists are asked to use the marked crossing.
items.note: Person riding a bicycle; signs often use the plural cyclists.

items.section: Signs and notices · Access and restrictions
items.example: The sign states that there is no admission without a ticket.
items.note: Admission means permission to enter a building, event or area.

items.section: Signs and notices · Access and restrictions
items.example: Admission is free for children under twelve.
items.note: In signs, admission refers to entry; it can also mean the price or permission to enter.

items.section: Signs and notices · Access and restrictions
items.example: Unaccompanied minors need written permission to join the tour.
items.note: A child under the relevant legal age who is not with a responsible adult; exact rules vary.

items.section: Signs and notices · Access and restrictions
items.example: A minor must be accompanied by an adult on this activity.
items.note: As a noun, minor refers to a child or young person below the legal age of adulthood.

items.section: Signs and notices · Access and restrictions
items.example: Visitors under sixteen must be accompanied by an adult.
items.note: Formal notice pattern: be accompanied by someone.

items.section: Signs and notices · Access and restrictions
items.example: The rules prohibit visitors from touching the exhibits.
items.note: Common formal pattern: prohibit someone from doing something.

items.section: Signs and notices · Access and restrictions
items.example: Photography is strictly prohibited in this room.
items.note: Strong sign wording meaning something is completely forbidden; strictly strengthens prohibited.

items.section: Signs and notices · Access and restrictions
items.example: Please refrain from talking during the performance.
items.note: Formal and polite: refrain from + noun or -ing form, not refrain to do.

items.section: Signs and notices · Access and restrictions
items.example: The audience entered the auditorium before the concert.
items.note: A room or hall where an audience sits to watch or listen.

items.section: Signs and notices · Access and restrictions
items.example: The door has a no entry notice for visitors.
items.note: No entry means access is not permitted; it also appears on one-way road signs.

items.section: Signs and notices · Access and restrictions
items.example: Unauthorised access to the laboratory is forbidden.
items.note: British spelling with s; US spelling unauthorized.

items.section: Signs and notices · Access and restrictions
items.example: Only trained personnel may operate the equipment.
items.note: Formal collective noun for staff; normally no plural personnels.

items.section: Signs and notices · Access and restrictions
items.example: Only permit holders may enter the restricted area.
items.note: A person who has a document giving permission for an activity or entry.

items.section: Signs and notices · Access and restrictions
items.example: You need a permit to park here overnight.
items.note: Noun has first-syllable stress; the verb permit commonly has second-syllable stress.

items.section: Signs and notices · Access and restrictions
items.example: This entrance is for staff only.
items.note: In notices, only places a restriction on a group of people or category.

items.pt: invasor de propriedade; pessoa que entra sem autorização
items.section: Signs and notices · Legal consequences and purchases
items.example: The sign warns trespassers not to enter the field.
items.note: A person entering land without permission; the legal consequences vary by jurisdiction.

items.pt: entrar sem permissão em propriedade alheia
items.section: Signs and notices · Legal consequences and purchases
items.example: Visitors must not trespass on the neighbouring land.
items.note: Common legal term for entering property without permission; not always a criminal offence.

items.section: Signs and notices · Legal consequences and purchases
items.example: The authorities may prosecute offenders under the relevant law.
items.note: To start or pursue a criminal case; a warning sign does not guarantee prosecution.

items.section: Signs and notices · Legal consequences and purchases
items.example: Anyone who commits fraud may be prosecuted.
items.note: Passive form common in warnings; legal action depends on the actual offence and local law.

items.section: Signs and notices · Legal consequences and purchases
items.example: There is a penalty for failing to pay the parking charge.
items.note: General punishment for breaking a rule, possibly a fine.

items.section: Signs and notices · Legal consequences and purchases
items.example: The company received a fine for breaching safety rules.
items.note: Money paid as a legal or administrative penalty; a fine is one type of penalty.

items.section: Signs and notices · Legal consequences and purchases
items.example: Visitors should place litter in the bins provided.
items.note: Litter means rubbish left in public places, not all household waste.

items.pt: jogar lixo no chão ou em local público
items.section: Signs and notices · Legal consequences and purchases
items.example: Residents can report drivers who drop litter from their cars.
items.note: Fixed collocation in public notices and regulations.

items.section: Signs and notices · Legal consequences and purchases
items.example: Breakfast is now being served in the dining room.
items.note: Formal service notice, common in cafés or hotels; present passive continuous.

items.section: Signs and notices · Legal consequences and purchases
items.example: Keep the receipt for your purchase.
items.note: Formal noun for buying something or an item that has been bought.

items.section: Signs and notices · Legal consequences and purchases
items.example: At the checkout, customers are asked to place their purchases here.
items.note: Polite instruction in shopping contexts; purchases refers to bought or selected goods.

items.pt: pessoa que furta mercadorias de uma loja
items.example: The security team reported a suspected shoplifter.
items.note: Someone who steals goods from a shop; differs from a normal customer.

items.example: Shoplifting can result in criminal charges.
items.note: A specific kind of theft involving taking items from a shop.

items.pt: falado aqui; idioma atendido neste local
items.example: The notice says that French is spoken here.
items.note: Common sign pattern identifying languages staff can use with customers.

items.example: She used the nothing to declare channel because she had no dutiable goods.
items.note: Customs expression indicating that travellers are not declaring goods requiring formal declaration.

items.example: You may need to declare expensive goods at customs.
items.note: Formal verb for reporting relevant goods or information to authorities.

items.pt: liquidação de estoque; queima de estoque
items.example: The department store held a clearance sale to make room for new products.
items.note: Sale to clear remaining stock; not necessarily evidence that the shop is closing permanently.

items.example: Ticket holders should use the main entrance.
items.note: A holder is a person who possesses the required ticket or document.

items.example: The guesthouse displayed a no vacancies sign throughout the weekend.
items.note: Can mean no available rooms or positions, depending on context.

items.example: The hotel has one vacancy for tonight.
items.note: A vacant job or an available room; notice meanings depend on the setting.

items.example: Fishing is prohibited in this part of the lake.
items.note: A compact notice omitting some ordinary sentence grammar.

items.example: Bicycles for hire are available next to the station.
items.note: British sign language for goods or equipment that customers can rent.

items.example: The flat is for sale, not for rent.
items.note: For sale means available to buy, not hire temporarily.

items.example: The landlord put up a sign saying that the flat was to let.
items.note: British property notice; let a property means rent it to a tenant.

items.example: Please keep priority seats available for passengers who need them.
items.note: Seats intended for people with greater accessibility needs; signage wording varies.

items.example: The notice asks passengers to offer seats to the elderly.
items.note: Collective adjective used as a noun; people of advanced age. People-first phrasing can be preferable in other contexts.

items.example: Pregnant passengers may need additional support when standing.
items.note: Adjective; use pregnant women or pregnant people when talking about individuals.

items.example: The notice says that unaccompanied minors cannot enter the event.
items.note: Formal signage for an age-related entry restriction; an accompanying adult may be required.

items.pt: entrada proibida para pessoas não autorizadas
items.example: Staff placed a no entry notice on the maintenance-room door.
items.note: Common access-warning wording; no entry for unauthorised personnel is also used.

items.example: Please refrain from handling the fragile displays.
items.note: Sign instruction: refrain from + -ing, especially when politely restricting contact.

units.title: Unit 100 — Headline English
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 100. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Newspaper headlines, compact news vocabulary and wordplay
learningObjectives: Recognise article and auxiliary omission and the present-simple or infinitive patterns of English headlines.
Understand short dramatic headline verbs and nouns and distinguish them from their ordinary uses.
Interpret abbreviations such as PM and MP in British news.
Explain headline puns based on homophones and multiple meanings.

sectionsChecked: Teaching page including illustrated signs or tables

items.example: The headline made the announcement sound more dramatic than it was.
items.note: Newspaper title designed to attract attention and summarise the news.

items.example: Headline English often sounds unusually compressed to learners.
items.note: Register used in headlines; it is not the normal style of everyday speech.

items.example: Editors may omit articles to make headlines shorter.
items.note: Headlines often leave out a, an and the; ordinary sentences generally need appropriate articles.

items.example: Short headlines may omit auxiliary verbs such as be or have.
items.note: Auxiliaries are often dropped in passive or perfect-like headline structures.

items.example: The headline uses the present simple although the announcement happened yesterday.
items.note: Present simple in a headline can describe a recent past event.

items.pt: infinitivo usado em manchetes para indicar futuro
items.example: A headline can use an infinitive to announce an upcoming visit.
items.note: To + base verb in a headline often signals a planned or future event.

items.example: Further cuts in energy prices are forecast for next month.
items.note: Forecast can be a noun or verb; headline grammar may omit is or are before it.

items.example: A local charity offered aid after the storm.
items.note: Short headline word for help; usable as a noun or verb.

items.example: The council may axe an unpopular scheme.
items.note: In headlines, axe means remove or cancel, often abruptly; also a noun.

items.example: Several MPs will back the proposed reform.
items.note: Headline verb meaning support, not move backwards.

items.example: The court may bar the company from selling the product.
items.note: Formal/headline verb for forbid or exclude; bar someone from doing something.

items.example: The team launched a bid to win the contract.
items.note: In news, a bid is an attempt, especially to achieve a goal.

items.example: A blast damaged several windows in the building.
items.note: Headline noun or verb for an explosion; can also mean criticise strongly elsewhere.

items.example: Firefighters responded to a large blaze at the warehouse.
items.note: A dramatic headline alternative to fire.

items.example: The new grant could boost local employment.
items.note: Can be a noun or verb, meaning increase or encouragement.

items.example: The firm's boss announced the expansion.
items.note: Short informal/headline word for manager or company leader.

items.example: A senior negotiator will head the delegation.
items.note: Headline verb means lead; a head can mean a leader.

items.example: The two groups clashed over the proposed changes.
items.note: Noun or verb for an argument or conflict, sometimes violent.

items.example: The new regulations aim to curb excessive fees.
items.note: Headline verb means control or limit; curb spending is a common collocation.

items.example: The bank announced a cut in borrowing costs.
items.note: Noun or verb for reducing; especially common with budgets, jobs and interest rates.

items.example: There was fresh drama during the negotiations.
items.note: In headline English, drama can refer to an unexpected or tense situation.

items.example: The city began a drive to improve recycling rates.
items.note: A noun in this sense: an organised campaign or push towards a goal.

items.example: Rare gems were recovered during the investigation.
items.note: In dramatic headlines, gems usually refers to jewels or precious stones.

items.example: The project received the go-ahead from the planning committee.
items.note: A noun meaning official permission or approval to proceed; usually the go-ahead.

items.example: Rising costs have hit small firms particularly hard.
items.note: Headline verb meaning harm or affect badly; not always a physical blow.

items.example: A key witness provided new evidence.
items.note: Headline adjective meaning essential or very important.

items.example: Investigators found a link between the two incidents.
items.note: Noun or verb for a connection; link A with B or link A to B.

items.example: The tax change was presented as a move to attract investment.
items.note: In headlines, move as a noun means a step or initiative, not just physical movement.

items.example: The passengers described a frightening ordeal at sea.
items.note: A painful, frightening or difficult experience.

items.example: Opposition members tried to oust the party leader.
items.note: Strong verb for removing someone from a position of power.

items.example: The charity issued a plea for more volunteers.
items.note: Often a public or emotional request, not a neutral request.

items.example: The mayor pledged to improve local transport.
items.note: Formal promise or commitment; pledge to do something.

items.example: Critics called the announcement a publicity ploy.
items.note: A clever or calculated tactic, sometimes intended to deceive.

items.example: A recent poll showed growing support for the plan.
items.note: May mean an opinion survey or election, depending on context.

items.example: The regulator opened a probe into the incident.
items.note: Headline noun or verb for a formal investigation.

items.pt: pedir demissão; deixar cargo ou atividade
items.example: The minister decided to quit after the report was published.
items.note: Headline verb for resign or leave a role; quit/quitted varies by sense, but quit is usual.

items.example: The sudden disappearance remains a riddle for investigators.
items.note: A puzzle or mystery; not necessarily a riddle told for amusement.

items.example: The region has experienced years of political strife.
items.note: Relatively formal word for long-running conflict, especially in public affairs.

items.example: Talks between the two organisations continued overnight.
items.note: Plural noun in diplomatic and political reporting; refers to discussions or negotiations.

items.example: Officials warned of a threat to public safety.
items.note: A danger or possibility of harm; death threat is a threat to kill someone.

items.example: The candidate vowed to publish the findings.
items.note: Dramatic/formal verb or noun for a strong promise.

items.example: The couple plan to wed in a small ceremony.
items.note: Short, formal or headline-style alternative to marry.

items.section: B · Abbreviations used in the news
items.example: The PM addressed Parliament about the agreement.
items.note: News abbreviation for Prime Minister; pronounced as separate letters, not like the time label in every context.

items.section: B · Abbreviations used in the news
items.example: An MP raised a question about transport funding.
items.note: Member of Parliament, especially in UK news; typically pronounced as separate letters.

items.section: B · Abbreviations used in the news
items.example: A Briton won the international science prize.
items.note: Mostly journalistic or formal noun for a British person; unlike Britain, it refers to a person.

items.example: The two sides discussed a new peace plan.
items.note: Headline collocation for a proposal intended to end a conflict.

items.pt: crise de espionagem; caso dramático envolvendo espiões
items.example: The minister was questioned during a spy drama involving confidential documents.
items.note: Drama means a tense or sensational situation here, not a theatre production.

items.example: A space probe sent back images of a distant asteroid.
items.note: Probe is a spacecraft here, unlike the investigative noun in political news.

items.example: The journalist reported a death threat to the police.
items.note: A threat to kill someone, not necessarily a completed attack.

items.pt: experiência traumática ou penosa no trabalho
items.example: The employee described her job ordeal during the hearing.
items.note: Headline-style compression; in normal prose, explain what difficult experience happened at work.

items.pt: hábitos de consumo; hábitos de gasto
items.example: The survey examined spending habits among younger adults.
items.note: The ways people typically use their money.

items.example: Lower interest rates may encourage more borrowing.
items.note: A familiar news collocation; use plural for rates across loans or markets.

items.pt: cortes cirúrgicos; redução de cirurgiões (em trocadilho)
items.example: The headline used surgical cuts as a pun about staffing reductions.
items.note: Pun on cuts meaning reductions and cuts made during surgery; quoted phrase is a wordplay example.

items.example: The cat folded its paws beneath its body.
items.note: Near-homophone of pause in many accents, useful for understanding the source headline pun.

items.example: The speaker left a dramatic pause before revealing the result.
items.note: Same sound as paws in standard British English, allowing a headline pun.

items.example: The royal heir attended the ceremony.
items.note: Sounds the same as air in many English accents; a source exercise uses this homophony.

items.example: The critics dismissed the announcement as hot air.
items.note: Idiom for empty claims or talk with little substance; contrasts with literal warm air.

items.example: The singer performed an aria from a famous opera.
items.note: A solo piece in opera; used for a joke involving rain and arias on the teaching page.

items.example: The editor used a pun in the newspaper headline.
items.note: Wordplay based on two meanings or on similar sounds.

items.example: The cartoonist likes to pun on people's surnames.
items.note: As a verb, pun means make a play on words; avoid confusing the verb and noun uses.
